paper.title_en: Hadronic cosmic-ray interactions in molecular clouds: Gamma-ray, neutrino, and secondary particle fluxes from a full six-species nuclear composition
paper.abstract_en: We present a geant4 Monte Carlo simulation of cosmic-ray (CR) hadronic interactions in a spherical molecular cloud (<math display="inline"><mo>∼</mo><mn>5400</mn><msub><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">⊙</mo></msub></math>, 13 concentric shells, <math display="inline"><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1.2</mn></mrow></msup></math> density profile) using six primary CR species, protons, alpha particles, carbon, oxygen, silicon, and iron, drawn from galprop-helmod local interstellar spectra over <math display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><mi>GeV</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi>nuc</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> to <math display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><mi>PeV</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi>nuc</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the hadronic interaction regime in which pion production and nuclear spallation dominate the secondary particle output. We compute, for the first time within this framework, radial energy deposition profiles, per-layer secondary production rates, and the differential physical flux of all emerging stable secondaries for the full nuclear CR composition. Energy deposition scales as <math display="inline"><msup><mi>Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, with the secondary cascade dominating <math display="inline"><mo>≥</mo><mn>92</mn><mo>%</mo></math> of the deposited energy in the dense core for all species. Alpha particles produce the highest integrated gamma-ray flux (<math display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.125</mn><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi>cm</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi>sr</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> above 100 MeV), followed by protons (<math display="inline"><mrow><mn>6.71</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi>cm</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi>sr</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>); together, they account for <math display="inline"><mo>≈</mo><mn>96</mn><mo>%</mo></math> of the total emerging gamma-ray and neutrino fluxes. A robust composition-diagnostic signature emerges in the neutrino sector: the <math display="inline"><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ν</mi><mo stretchy="false">¯</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub></math> ratio above 100 MeV decreases from <math display="inline"><mo>≈</mo><mn>6.4</mn></math> for protons, driven by the <math display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><msup><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo></mrow></msup><mo>≈</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>–</mi><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> charge asymmetry, to <math display="inline"><mo>≈</mo><mn>2.8</mn></math> for <math display="inline"><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Z</mi></math> nuclei (C, O, Si), directly encoding the isospin content of the primary CR beam in an observable flux ratio. Secondary nuclear clusters (<math display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>, <math display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>, <math display="inline"><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></math>, <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>, and heavier ions up to <math display="inline"><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></math>) emerge exclusively for nuclei heavier than protons, contributing at the <math display="inline"><mo>≈</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>%</mo></math> level of the secondary proton flux for light clusters, while heavy-ion fragments remain 1 to 2 orders of magnitude below the secondary proton channel.
